title: The Witch of Endor and the Limits of Demons
english: A runner, having stripped off his clothes, left the army. When he arrived at her at night with two men, he approached her with such requests, saying, 'Prophesy to me through the belly-speaker and bring up for me'—he says—'whomever I may tell you.' Truly, if Saul was seen to prophesy through the belly-speaker, someone might say his voices were true. But is there anyone unaware that he was driven by wild passions by a demon, turned toward unlawful divination and diabolical myth-working?

For is not God more trustworthy, having cast the words into the mouth of Balaam (Numbers 22:28), but having permitted Moses to write explicitly in Numbers: 'For there is no enchantment against Jacob, nor divination against Israel' (Numbers 23:23)? If such things are to be forbidden, such as these secret abominations and causes of the enemy's idolatry, how could the witness be worthy, having used these most impious things when tempted? But these things, having repeated them a little later more perfectly, we shall say; yet we must return again to the history of the letter.

As the woman saw the irrational Saul, pretending not to know the ruler, she was more distressed as if it would be better for her to know what terrible things Saul was doing regarding these matters, saying, 'How he has destroyed the belly-speakers and those crying out from the earth.' Because of this, she said she would ensnare his soul unto death. And since, having been convinced by an oath, he confirmed that he would not support any trickery, the woman, immediately being emboldened by the wickedness, answers more boldly from somewhere: 'Whom shall I bring up to you?'

What sort of and what kind of and who was this evil-demon old woman, so that she might promise to bring up Samuel from the dead? And indeed, if it is necessary to say the things exceeding their worth, she was not able to bring up a prophetic soul even if she could have, nor even any of those who succeed, nor at all, not even an ant or a flea. For the demons do not have authority over spirits and souls, but God, the Lord of all things together; so that by divine giving alone, it is possible for souls to pass from Hades and to be called up again.

But the elegant Origenes, desiring to surround the church with a dance of idolatrous instruments and necromantic findings, is refuted by the divine letter. For the scripture's voice cries out clearly, as the woman said, 'Whom shall I bring up to you?' (1 Sam 28:13); on the contrary, this man, turning it around, said the face [of the text] spoke these things of the Holy Spirit.

Then he was so led astray, being seduced, that he did not hesitate to treat the words of the one possessed with holy respect; but blaspheming more nakedly with the tongue, he attributes the whole matter to the Holy Spirit, attempting to insult the listeners by name as untrustworthy.

The woman indeed spoke, as I said, and as having authority to bring the dead up, she cries out: 'Whom,' she says, 'shall I bring up to you?' (1 Sam 28:13); and when the one divining said that Samuel had been raised, she immediately brings forth: 'And the woman saw Samuel,' she said, 'and she cried out with a great voice and said' (1 Sam 28:14) to the ruler, 'Why have you perturbed me? And you are Saul' (1 Sam 28:15). How then the king said to her, 'Do not fear' and added, 'What have you seen?' (1 Sam 28:15); immediately the pythomist countered again, saying: 'I have seen gods ascending from the earth' (1 Sam 28:15). And since the ruler also asked the last thing, 'What did you know?', she immediately again responded with the words, 'A righteous man ascending from the earth, and this one, having been cast down, is double' (1 Sam 28:15). Why then does the divine scripture forbid this? 'And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed down with his face to the earth and worshiped him' (1 Sam 28:20). It appears, therefore, that nowhere at all does the interpretation of the divine letter declare that Samuel was brought up by the medium; but she previously, through the demon erupting from her, speaks that it is necessary to bring him up; then she is seen approaching gods ascending, and through deception she gave the signs of the man into a trance, but the one misinterpreting says 'Saul knew' (1 Sam 28:20) from which he heard that this one is Samuel.

If it is necessary to believe either that Saul, the demonized one, had a grasp of true knowledge, or a demon swelling with pride and promising to bring the souls of the righteous from Hades, let us judge for ourselves how much of a reputation these and such things would bring, which even the mightiest of men, EuTropius, would [avoid]. For much, as it seems, is the error of Origenes regarding the truth, even though our Lord Jesus has spoken clearly concerning the devil, 'He was a murderer from the beginning, and in the truth [he was not found]' (John 8:44).

title: The Demon and the Narrator's Voice
english: He stands, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own nature, saying that he is a liar and so is his father. So what are you saying, O Origen, since it is necessary to ask you? Are these things which the Savior expressed true, or will you say the opposite, countering them? If indeed the words of the Lord happen to be true, then the demon has habitually lied, becoming insolent; but if you define the words of the demon as being without falsehood, you attempt to declare the Lord a liar.

Do you see how far the dogmatizing rule being presented to you has fallen into absurdity? For demons are indeed powerless when they are forced to speak the truth, being twisted by pains, not willingly speaking anything without falsehood. And if someone defines this one as raising a righteous man out of Hades without delay, how could it not be clear that the lie opposes it, desiring to throw someone aside?

Yes, he says, but not the demon has said these things, but 'the narrative voice of the writer'; and the writer of the words is believed to be the Holy Spirit, not a man. Do you not perceive how this appears contrary to the mode of the narrative? It is better, indeed, that those who have spoken with words more suited to all kinds of leisure know that the narrative voice of the writer brought these things forth, as the possessed Saul seemed to do or say; the writer, neglecting that distinction and setting the words of it out literally, said, 'And the woman said: What shall I bring up to you?'

Who is so pleasant as to pretend not to perceive that these are not the voices of the writer, but are of the woman being possessed, whose name also he put forward? Yet he nowhere confirms her words as true, nor could anyone be able to demonstrate this at all. But truly, if it must be said lovingly, the narrative voice said this only as 'the woman saw Samuel.' Thus he wrote these things as one speaking to those who know about possessed speech. For there is no disputing that a demon does not raise the soul of anyone, who, being exorcised by pious men, is driven away, burned, scourged, and flees, leaving the tent behind. But the misled woman saw the form of the apparition as was proper for her.

For the beast is accustomed to changing its appearance into many faces. Thus, after speaking the words of the holy Paul: 'for Satan himself transforms into an angel of light; it is no great thing, if his servants also transform as servants of righteousness' (2 Cor 11:14; 2 Cor 6:7).

The dogmatist Origen, debating opponents with legalistic cunning, also arranged this passage, thinking he describes those who oppose the truth, but he seems to be reconstructing it more by lack of skill than by art. He asks, 'And why' it is not said: 'the woman saw a demon who pretended to be Samuel?' but he said it had been written thus: 'Saul knew that Samuel is' (1 Sam 28:13); then again he brings forward: 'if Samuel had not been, it should have been written; and Saul thought he was Samuel.' Now it is written: 'Saul knew.' But no one knew what does not exist; 'Saul knew that Samuel is and fell on his face upon the earth and worshiped him.'

In order not to go beyond other examples—from those which I have written here I will make the question, and thus I will walk through the remaining examples—he says to God: 'What are you saying, Origen? Whether the woman brought Samuel to him in body, or what kind of shadow-form she saw wrapped around him?' If indeed she brought him incorporeal, she did not raise up Samuel, but an appearance of a spirit; for he who is joined of soul and body is this Samuel, the man having a proportion analogous from both.

But if she brought the man entirely in body, how did Saul not see him? For if he had seen him with his own eyes, he would not have questioned the woman as if seeing one invisible, saying 'what did you see?' in his own words. For if he were invisible, it is indisputable he was incorporeal; but if he appeared in an incorporeal form, why did the prophetess at times declare the opposite, to have seen 'a man standing upright coming up out of the earth,' and 'a double [form]' according to the custom mentioned before, 'wrapped around' him? Therefore, fight these same things with your words, Origen; for Saul, not having seen anything at all and debating as if concerning an invisible phantom, asked 'what did you see?'; but she, seeing him as a man, cried out 'a man standing upright coming up out of the earth,' in order to persuade that he himself [...]

title: The nature of the vision
english: He is a man, and she gives him a sign by pronouncing, 'and this one appeared double-faced.' If the hypotheses of unlawful divination happened to be a man, did Saul not see him? Unless you would say that the sensible eye was made blind for him, just as the intelligible part of the intellect was also neglected.

But perhaps you will say, being pleasantly mocked: the very organ of the soul was shaped anthropomorphically according to the hour, so that it might declare the future with a manifest prophetic message, just as sometimes spirits and souls stand over men in dreams, showing human characters most intently; not indeed, but bearing various and diverse garments and signs of scales or types or blemishes or wounds.

If, therefore, you determine that a soul is to be carried up only, but not a man with his body (for he does not give you the letter if he wishes), fighting against himself and devising things without perceiving, someone else bearing this against you will say: 'When did the woman say: I saw a prophetic soul, but on the contrary, an upright man?' For he spoke to you in such a way: 'And why,' saying, 'is it not said: the woman saw a demon pretending to be Samuel?' With this word I would have appeared to have countered you: for what reason, if it were so, has she not said she saw a soul, but instead from the opposites, a 'man' and this 'upright one', which is a sign of bodily well-being?

For the madwoman did not say she saw a man who was bent or stooped, but an upright one, tense, directed toward war, always fresh around the cycles of evil; and deceiving the fool by a falsehood, she first persuaded him by a sign that the one coming from the earth is a man, but it seemed that he had appeared 'double-faced.' So what (if someone were to say), if he happened to appear as a man with his body, did Saul not then see him, but does he wish to learn from another what kind of man he is, having been struck by invisibility? Surely the facts have cried out that he was not a man, but some kind of shadow that seemed invisible; for he would not have been invisible.

But if you think, Origen, that the soul of Samuel happened to be there, why then was the apparition seen being enwrapped in double [clothing]? For it is clearly made manifest by the significance that all the garments and coverings of the raiment are more for bodies than for souls. For I do not suppose you would say, without hypocrisy and wavering, that the double [clothing] has remained upon the tomb for so many days until this very day, so that the soul of the prophet might wear it, lest it should perhaps wander about walking naked. Even if someone were to say that no one is so ignorant as to not know that for the saints there are incorruptible garments from heaven, shining with light-bearing gleams, they are not fabrics of raiment of various colors.

If, however, you define the one seen to be the soul of Samuel, yet you say that a priestly garment is seen according to a concept, in order that the manner of the liturgy might be manifest (though both these things are properties of mental things), it has come to pass that the madwoman reported nothing healthy or true. For she was saying other things apart from what actually exists, misrepresenting the names of sensible things and demonstrating the matters of the intelligible. For instance, calling a 'man' an 'upright [garment],' and introducing an invisible, phantom-like spirit through the opposite of a hand-woven garment of clothing.

Tell me then, O best of dogmatists, how did Saul know that this very person happened to be Samuel, when he saw not even a fragment of a shadow, not even an image of a man? But you have not spoken correctly: 'It was necessary that it be written; and Saul thought that he was Samuel. But now it has been written: "Saul knew"' [1 Sam 28:13-15]. Furthermore, that the demonized man knew by hearing from the demonizing woman, you say both above and below; but that he did not see at all, you hide in silence. You do not bring the refutation into the midst anywhere; you seem to set aside [the truth] thinking to deceive men, yet you prop up a finding of divination against all the ungodly. For the knowledge of the demonized man was of the value of the proclamation of her who was also ministering the words to him.

But with skill and understanding, you would say that he knew without seeing, but rather he thought so. For every man receives a matter more by hearing than by sight and thinks and supposes it, not knowing the clear truth, even if he hears it from a person being demonized; for only the words of God are established for precise apprehension and the strength of faith. And indeed, if the diviner said concerning men: 'I said in my ecstasy: every man is a liar' [Ps 146:6], how much...
